desc:
You are given an integer array nums and an inclusive interval [lo, hi]. The array is unsorted, may contain repeated values, and may contain values outside the interval, which must simply be ignored.

Every integer in lo..hi that does not occur in nums is missing. Group the missing integers into maximal blocks of consecutive integers and return them as a list of [start, end] pairs (both inclusive), sorted by start. If nothing is missing, return an empty list.

For example, nums = [5, 3, 50, 9, 3, 75], lo = 3, hi = 60 gives [[4, 4], [6, 8], [10, 49], [51, 60]].
constraints: lo ≤ hi (the interval can be huge, so do not loop over all of its integers)
hints: The interval can contain billions of integers, so you cannot test them one by one. Work with the values that are present instead.
Keep only the values inside [lo, hi], remove repeats, and sort them. Missing blocks can only sit between neighbouring present values.
Track prev, starting at lo - 1. For each present value x in order (and finally for hi + 1 as a sentinel), if x - prev > 1 then [prev + 1, x - 1] is a missing block; then set prev = x.
editorial: After filtering to the interval and deduplicating (a set does both jobs), sort the surviving values. The integers between two consecutive present values, and between the interval ends and the first or last present value, are exactly the missing blocks.

Starting with prev = lo - 1 and ending with the sentinel hi + 1 unifies the three kinds of gaps into one rule: whenever the next value is more than one above prev, emit [prev + 1, next - 1]. The cost is dominated by sorting, O(n log n), and the output has at most n + 1 blocks. Because the interval may span the full 32-bit range, the algorithm must never iterate over the interval itself.
